source: Wyrich, Bogner, Wagner (2024) 40 Years of Designing Code Comprehension Experiments
finding: Systematic map of 95 code comprehension experiments, 1979-2019. The field has no shared design: tasks, measures and snippets differ widely, so results are hard to compare or replicate.
numbers: 95 studies; 94 of 95 are experiments; participants 5 to 277, median 34 (journals median 61, conferences 26); 53.7% students only, 9.5% professionals only; 71% on screen, 76% onsite; median snippet pool 9; 71 of 94 one-factor-at-a-time designs.
limits: Mapping study, not a meta-analysis: no pooled effect sizes. Only bottom-up comprehension studies up to 2019.
agent_relevance: Human claims about reading code rest on small student samples with non-standard tasks. Use them as hints for scaffold design, not as tuned constants.

source: Wyrich, Bogner, Wagner (2024) 40 Years of Designing Code Comprehension Experiments
finding: Most studies test which construct influences comprehension. Popular topics are semantic cues (identifier names, comments), developer traits, and code structure. Eye tracking, fMRI and EEG work is a growing but small slice.
numbers: 67 of 95 (71%) study 'X influences comprehension'; 81% use at least one task where the participant gives information about the snippet; 28.4% use personal ratings; 7 papers say 'readability' but measured understanding.
limits: Labels assigned by the authors with a four-eyes check; some inclusion judgments were subjective.
agent_relevance: Measures conflate self-rating with correct answers. Our agent should score comprehension only by checked answers (G2, G3), never by self-reported confidence.

source: Wyrich, Bogner, Wagner (2024) 40 Years of Designing Code Comprehension Experiments
finding: Snippet choice is driven by a balance between simple and hard. Many studies force bottom-up reading by obfuscating identifiers and removing beacons and comments.
numbers: 42 of 95 studies used 'not too easy, not too hard' as the main snippet criterion; 25 selected for novice friendliness.
limits: Small, short snippets. Real systems are far larger.
agent_relevance: Results come from toy snippets. Transfer to repository-scale agent reading is untested.

source: Wyrich, Bogner, Wagner (2024) 40 Years of Designing Code Comprehension Experiments
finding: Design weaknesses in the field: student-only samples, short snippets, subjective measures. Few studies use factorial designs, which are needed to estimate moderators such as expertise.
numbers: 53.7% students only; only 23 of 94 experiments used factorial designs.
limits: Limitations were extracted from the papers, not independently re-analysed.
agent_relevance: Moderators (expertise, time pressure, culture) are largely untested in crossed designs. Do not hard-code expertise-dependent rules.

source: Peitek, Siegmund, Apel et al. (2018) Neural efficiency of top-down program comprehension (fMRI replication of Siegmund 2014)
finding: fMRI replication of an earlier bottom-up comprehension study. Reading with semantic cues gave lower activation in language and working-memory areas than bottom-up reading, which fits the idea that cues make comprehension cheaper.
numbers: 11 participants; Brodmann areas 6, 21, 39, 40, 44, 47; bottom-up vs semantic-cue conditions; the earlier activation pattern was reproduced.
limits: N=11; participants studied the cue snippets before scanning, so 'cues' also means familiarity; fMRI is indirect.
agent_relevance: Informative names lower comprehension cost. Supports a scaffold step that restores or adds meaningful names or summaries before reasoning about code.

source: Peitek, Siegmund, Apel et al. (2018) Neural efficiency of top-down program comprehension (fMRI replication of Siegmund 2014)
finding: Beacons did not separately change activation, and layout (pretty vs disrupted) did not matter in the key areas. The classic beacon story is not confirmed at the neural level.
numbers: 2x2 beacon x layout design; no difference across the four variants in BA 21; no significant beacon effect reported.
limits: Null result with N=11 has little power; authors say the theory could be wrong or beacons were not as defined.
agent_relevance: Do not assume 'find the beacon line' is a reliable mechanism.

source: Peitek, Siegmund, Apel et al. (2018) Neural efficiency of top-down program comprehension (fMRI replication of Siegmund 2014)
finding: Supports semantic chunking in bottom-up comprehension (BA 39, an integration hub, active) and is consistent with successive hypothesis refinement in cue-based comprehension (BA 39 below rest).
numbers: BA 39 more active in bottom-up than semantic-cue condition; response times did not differ between strategies.
limits: Reverse inference from brain area to process is weak.
agent_relevance: Two modes: bottom-up chunking when cues are missing, hypothesis-driven when cues exist. An agent can pick the mode by cue quality.

source: Peitek, Apel, Parnin, Brechmann, Siegmund (2021) Program Comprehension and Code Complexity Metrics: An fMRI Study
finding: Classic complexity metrics predict comprehension cost only partly. McCabe cyclomatic complexity showed no correlation with response time, correctness or brain activation. LOC, Halstead vocabulary and DepDegree (data flow) showed small to medium correlations.
numbers: 19 participants, 16 Java snippets chosen from 50; 72% solved correctly, mean 32 s per task; Kendall tau bands: small 0.1-0.3, medium 0.3-0.5; McCabe near 0; LOC, Halstead, DepDegree small on time and medium on correctness.
limits: Scanner screen size limited snippets so metrics correlated with each other; short snippets; 19 people.
agent_relevance: Do not use cyclomatic complexity as the trigger for 'hard to understand' code. Size and vocabulary are better cheap signals.

source: Peitek, Apel, Parnin, Brechmann, Siegmund (2021) Program Comprehension and Code Complexity Metrics: An fMRI Study
finding: Text size works as a preattentive cue: more lines gave stronger default-mode-network deactivation, so people brace for work before reading. Vocabulary size adds working-memory load.
numbers: 37 further metrics explored (text says 37; the repository page says 41); Halstead most consistent across areas; simple control-flow counts (branch count, max loop depth) correlated more than McCabe.
limits: Exploratory search over many metrics raises false-positive risk.
agent_relevance: Cheap signals the program can compute (token count, distinct identifiers, nesting depth) can trigger chunked reading.

source: Peitek, Apel, Parnin, Brechmann, Siegmund (2021) Program Comprehension and Code Complexity Metrics: An fMRI Study
finding: Post-task subjective complexity rating separated solved from unsolved snippets and tracked cognitive load better than metrics.
numbers: Subjective complexity had small correlation with metrics but matched whether the task was solved.
limits: Rating was given after solving, which differs from judging before acting.
agent_relevance: Only supports post-run ratings. Our schema already forbids self-grading without a check (G2).

source: Wyrich, Preikschat, Graziotin, Wagner (2021) The Mind Is a Powerful Place: How Showing Code Comprehensibility Metrics Influences Code Understanding
finding: A displayed comprehensibility metric anchored developers' subjective ratings strongly but did not change their accuracy or time.
numbers: 43 MSc students (easy-anchor n=20, hard-anchor n=23); t(40.318)=-4.227, p=.000132, d=-1.29, 95% CI [-1.97,-0.61] on ratings; no significant effect on correctness or time; anchoring weaker for optimistic and conscientious people.
limits: Convenience student sample; three Java methods; the shown metric was unvalidated by design.
agent_relevance: Self-reported ease is manipulable by a shown number while true performance is not. Do not let an earlier score or label anchor the agent's ease judgement.

source: Langhout, Aniche (2021) Atoms of Confusion in Java
finding: Replication of Gopstein's C 'atoms of confusion' in Java. Half of the atoms raised misreading; others showed no effect, so the original result replicates only partly.
numbers: 132 CS students, two phases; 2.7 up to 56 times more likely to err on 7 of 14 atoms; pooled odds ratio 3.82 (95% CI 2.69 to 5.42); 10 of 14 atoms judged more confusing in forced choice; infix precedence and indentation atoms not significant.
limits: Novice students; atoms re-derived for Java. The abstract says 2.7 to 56 and the conclusion says 4.6 to 56, an inconsistency in the paper.
agent_relevance: Specific misreading traps exist. A scaffold can test such constructs by execution instead of reading.

source: Noone, Mooney (2018) Beacons and Novice Programming Comprehension (eye tracking, phase 1)
finding: Eye-tracking heat maps from non-novices suggested candidate beacon lines: multiple if conditions, loop calculation points, nested loop bounds. The paper also recounts that experts use beacons, novices much less, and poor names block novices.
numbers: 10 Java examples; 5 pilot subjects, 24 main participants; beacons inferred from dwell time where correct participants shared fixations.
limits: Small exploratory paper; no statistics on beacon effects; Wiedenbeck and Crosby results are secondhand.
agent_relevance: Beacon claims are mostly descriptive. Treat loop accumulation lines as likely focus points, not a proven mechanism.

source: Wiedenbeck (1986) Beacons in computer program comprehension (as cited by Noone and Mooney)
finding: Original beacon study: experienced programmers recognise typical code structures from indicator lines; novices do not.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not recorded.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Backward link for the Brooks/Soloway line; needs full-text pass before use.

source: Brooks (1983) Towards a theory of the comprehension of computer programs
finding: Top-down theory: programmers form hypotheses from domain knowledge and refine them against code; beacons confirm or reject them.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Cited only.
agent_relevance: Gives the hypothesis-refinement loop that our hypothesis operators mirror; neural evidence is weak.

source: Siegmund et al. (2014) Understanding understanding source code with functional MRI (as cited in Peitek 2018)
finding: First fMRI study of bottom-up comprehension; Peitek 2018 replicates it.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Baseline that the 2018 replication reproduced.

source: Paltenghi, Pradel et al. (2024) Follow-Up Attention: An Empirical Study of Developer and Neural Model Code Exploration (ICSE 2025 journal-first)
finding: Eye-tracking study of 25 developers on sensemaking questions. Code models (CodeGen, InCoder, GPT-J) agree with developers on where to look next only when attention is processed as 'follow-up attention'.
numbers: 25 developers, 92 valid sessions; developer answers correct or partly correct in almost 70%; models 39.3% (CodeGen), 36.3% (GPT-J), 37.7% (InCoder); next-line prediction 47% vs 42.3% baseline from other developers' histories; language gap up to 13.3 points.
limits: Small 2022-era open models; zero-shot; volunteers with varied experience; aggregation across people is noisy.
agent_relevance: Navigation has some shared structure, but the gain is small (+4.7 points). Weak prior for choosing which function to open next.

source: Li, Zhang, Karas, McMillan, Leach, Huang (2024) Do Machines and Humans Focus on Similar Code? (ICPC 2024)
finding: Negative result: black-box LLM feature attribution (SHAP) does not correlate with programmer eye fixations during code summarisation, for six models.
numbers: 27 programmers, 671 trials, 68 Java methods; GPT-4, GPT-3.5, GPT-few-shot, StarCoder, Code Llama, NCS; only 22% of methods had any significant human-model Spearman correlation; baseline: human duration and count agreed on all methods and 85% of model-model pairs agreed; models lean on comments and return values.
limits: SHAP may be the wrong probe; summarisation, not debugging; summary quality was independent of alignment.
agent_relevance: Good output does not need human-like attention. Do not force the agent to mimic human reading order.

source: Kou, Chen, Wang, Ma, Zhang (2024) Do LLMs Pay Similar Attention Like Human Programmers When Generating Code? (FSE 2024)
finding: Consistent misalignment between six LLMs' attention and programmers' attention on task descriptions. Five attention patterns explain part of wrong code.
numbers: 6 LLMs incl. GPT-4; 1,138 tasks from HumanEval and MBPP labelled by 2 programmers; Krippendorff alpha below 0.3 and F1 below 0.6 for every model, GPT-4 lowest overlap; 57 of 211 wrong solutions (27%) explained by a pattern; 22 students preferred perturbation-based explanations.
limits: Task descriptions only, not code reading; human attention approximated by two labelers' keyword marks.
agent_relevance: Models skip words people treat as key. A restatement step that lists key constraints targets this gap.

source: Zhang, Huang, Karas, Nguyen, Leach, Huang (2025) Enhancing Code LLM Training with Programmer Attention
finding: Using eye-tracking scanpaths to reweight fine-tuning improves CodeT5 on summarisation and completion.
numbers: 15 professional developers read 120 Java methods; up to +7.16 CodeBLEU and +2.67 Syntax on CodeXGlue; 10% sample of each dataset; single seed 42.
limits: Small sample, one seed, one model, similarity metrics only; training-based.
agent_relevance: Out of scope for a scaffold; shows human attention data has signal but not that it improves reliability.

source: Elfares, Calikli, Khamis (2025) GazeCopilot: Gaze-Informed Prompting for AI-Supported Code Comprehension and Readability
finding: Prompts built from live gaze data made Copilot-refactored code easier to understand than a standard prompt. A fixed 'struggling everywhere' prompt did not beat standard.
numbers: 25 developers, 3 snippets; mean comprehension gain 1.44 (SD 0.77) real-time vs 1.32 pre-set vs 0.56 standard; real-time vs standard p=.0122, rank-biserial r=.220; real-time vs pre-set p=.0137, r=.698; 64% ranked real-time most readable.
limits: Lab study, score range 0 to 2, no main effect of mode (p=.496), only an interaction with version.
agent_relevance: Targeting changes to the parts the reader struggles with beats rewriting everything. Matches G1 and G2: act where a signal says so.

source: Wei, Cao, Li et al. (2025) EquiBench: Benchmarking LLMs' Reasoning about Program Semantics via Equivalence Checking
finding: On deciding whether two programs behave the same, 19 LLMs do poorly on hard categories and lean on surface similarity. Few-shot and chain-of-thought barely help.
numbers: 2400 pairs, 4 languages, 6 categories; best overall 82.3% (o4-mini); hardest categories best 63.8% and 76.2% vs 50% chance; CUDA 60.8% for the best model; variable renaming up to 96.5%; accuracy rises with syntactic similarity on equivalent pairs (alpha 0.05); LoRA fine-tune Qwen2.5-14B 59.8% to 63.2% on 1,200 examples.
limits: Synthetic transformation pairs; binary task.
agent_relevance: Model judgments of 'same behaviour' follow syntax. The agent should test equivalence by running inputs (G3).

source: Roy, Kaiser, Chen, Steenhoek, Ray, Peng, Le (2026) CodeSense: A Real-World Benchmark for Code Semantic Reasoning
finding: Fine-grained reasoning about execution (values, aliasing, branch feasibility, loop properties) on real projects is weak. Chain-of-thought and in-context examples help only somewhat.
numbers: 14 LLMs (8 reasoning, 6 non-reasoning); on C, Claude 3.5 and GPT-4o-mini under 30% accuracy on single-statement blocks; input prediction consistently poor; yes/no questions (aliasing, branch taken) easier than loop properties.
limits: Tests prediction by reading, not tool-supported runs; 2024-25 models.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that 'read and predict' is the weak step. Behaviour claims should come from real execution output.

source: Nguyen Manh et al. (2025) CodeMMLU: A Multi-Task Benchmark for Code Understanding and Reasoning (ICLR 2025)
finding: On nearly 20,000 multiple-choice code understanding questions strong models struggle. Chain-of-thought gave no clear gain on knowledge questions, and answer position changed results.
numbers: ~20,000 questions; repair, execution reasoning, fill-in-the-blank; permuting the correct option changed accuracy markedly (Table 7, Fig. 9); CoT-fixed questions showed no pattern.
limits: Multiple-choice format with position bias; single runs.
agent_relevance: Fits G1: extra reasoning is not a reliable gain for code understanding. Randomise option order when the agent compares options.

source: Search coverage note for this file
finding: Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv search APIs were rate limited in this run, so Brooks 1983, Letovsky 1986, Busjahn 2015 linearity, Hofmeister 2017 identifier names and the ICSE 2025 reading-strategy paper were not opened. No large preregistered replication of Brooks or Letovsky was found in the sources read.
numbers: Replications read: fMRI N=11 (reproduced), atoms of confusion N=132 (7 of 14 atoms replicated).
limits: Absence in what I read is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Open items for a later pass.
